blocks.text: Some obscure passages of Scripture on Locusts are explained.

One may ask why, in the class of locusts or bruchi, the ילק jelek is called סמר samar, Ierem. LI, 27., that is, φρίττων [phrittōn], bristling, or ὀρθόθριξ [orthothrix], horripilans [with hair standing on end], one whose hair stands erect with horror. So Iob. IV, 15. When a spirit passed before me; תסמר שערת בשרי, the hairs of my flesh stood up. And Psal. CXIX, 120. סמר מפחדך בשרי, My flesh bristled for fear of thee. Here Symmachus has ὀρθοτριχεῖ [orthotrichei], and the Syriac ܣܦܣ? — an elegant verb formed from the Hebrew noun קפוד, which means hedgehog. In the same way we say in French herisser, not from horrescere [to bristle], as some would have it, but from this very animal, which we call un herisson. The ancient Romans expressed it by a periphrasis, as the Poet:
I was stunned, and my hair stood on end. — —

But a later age said horripilare and horripilatio. Apuleius, in his third book, speaking of himself when changed into an ass: My ears bristle with immoderate growth. The old Glossaries: Horripilatur, ὀρθοτριχεῖ [orthotrichei]. The lexicon of Philoxenus: Ὀρθοτριχιῶ [orthotrichiō], horripilo. The Vulgate translator, Eccesiast. XXVII, 15.: Speech that swears much (I would read of one who swears much, as the Greek Λαλιὰ πολυόρκου [Lalia polyorkou]) will make the hair of the head stand on end, in Greek ὀρθώσει τρίχας [orthōsei trichas]. This condition does not seem applicable to a locust or a bruchus, since they are hairless. Therefore Castalio, Petrus Robertus, the English translators, and perhaps many others render it eruca [caterpillar], a very hairy little creature. Hence Columella in the Garden:
Nor do the slug wrapped in its shell and the hairy campedare to gnaw only the tender leaves.

Campe, that is, eruca, as he himself explains in his prose On the Cultivation of the Garden, near the end of book 12: Those which we call ERUCAE are named in Greek κάμπαι [kampai]. But one feature is not enough to establish this rendering when the others are lacking: for instance flight in the caterpillar, which is attributed to the jelek in Nahum III, 16. ילק פשט ויעף, Ielek spread itself out and flew away. Jerome elegantly, on chapter 4 of Amos: The caterpillar does not fly away like the locust, etc., but remains on the crops that are to perish, and with slow movement and sluggish bites consumes everything. Moreover, that Jeremiah compares the masses of horsemen rushing with great force upon the Babylonians to the bristling jelek [III, 272] does not seem to fit the caterpillar, which has nothing to resemble hostile bands.

Accordingly, for Junius and Tremellius ילק jelek is neither locust nor caterpillar, but melolontha, a little creature of which Hesychius says: Μηλολόνθη· εἶδος κανθάρων, οὓς τινες χρυσοκανθάρους λέγουσι [Mēlolonthē; eidos kantharōn, hous tines chrysokantharous legousi]. It is called melolontha, namely, because it is the bane of fruit; and chrysocantharus, as it were golden beetle, because it resembles a beetle in shape and gold in colour. Hence Aristophanes too, in the Wasps, calls it χρυσομηλολόνθιον [chrysomēlolonthion]. There the Scholiast: Ζωΰφιόν τί ἐστι κατὰ κάνθαρον ξανθὸν, ὃ καὶ κατέχοντες οἱ παῖδες δεσμοῦσιν ἐκ τοῦ ποδὸς, καὶ ἀφιᾶσι πρὸς τὸν ἀέρα [Zōyphion ti estin kata kantharon xanthon, ho kai katechontes hoi paides desmousin ek tou podos, kai aphiasi pros ton aera]; It is a little creature like a beetle, tawny, which boys catch, tie by the foot, and let go into the air. To this belong these lines of the same Aristophanes in the Clouds:
Ἀλλ᾽ ἀποχάλα τὴν φροντίδ᾽ ἐς τὸν ἀέρα, Λινόδετον ὥσπερ μηλολόνθην τοῦ ποδός· [All' apochala tēn phrontid' es ton aera, Linodeton hōsper mēlolonthēn tou podos;]
